title: I committed to main by mistake
summary: The commit is on the wrong branch. What you do next depends entirely on whether it has been pushed.

steps.title: Find out whether the commit has left your machine
steps.look: The first line. 'ahead 1' means it is still local and you have easy options. If it is not ahead, it is already on the remote and rewriting is now other people's problem too.

signals.means: Still local. You can move it cleanly.
Already pushed. Do not rewrite shared history.

steps.title: Move the commit onto the branch it belonged on
steps.cmd: git branch {branch} && git reset --hard HEAD~1 && git switch {branch}
steps.note: reset --hard discards every uncommitted change in your working tree. Run git stash first if you have any. This is only safe because git branch {branch} was created on the line before, so the commit itself survives on that branch.
steps.look: After this, main is back where it was and your commit sits on {branch}.

signals.means: That branch already exists. Pick another name or switch to it and cherry-pick instead.

steps.title: Confirm nothing was lost
steps.look: Your commit on {branch}, and main matching the remote. If anything looks wrong, git reflog still has every prior position for about 90 days.

causes.cause: The commit exists only in your clone.
causes.fix: Create the branch at the current commit, then reset main back one. Nobody else is affected.

causes.cause: The commit is on the remote and others may have pulled it.
causes.fix: Do not reset and force-push. Use git revert to add a new commit that undoes it, then apply the original work on a proper branch.

causes.cause: A branch with that name is already present.
causes.fix: Switch to it and cherry-pick the commit across, then reset main.

verify: git log on main matches the remote's main.
Your commit appears in git log on {branch}.
git status reports a clean working tree, or exactly the changes you stashed.
escalate: Whether the commit was pushed, and whether anyone has pulled since

title: I need to force-push a rebased branch
summary: Rewriting a shared branch can silently destroy a colleague's commits. There is a safe form of this command.

steps.title: Check whether anyone else has pushed to this branch
steps.look: Commits you do not recognise. If someone else's work is on this branch, a force-push will delete it and they will not get a warning.

signals.means: Read the author of each. Anything not yours means stop and talk to them first.

steps.title: Force-push, but only if the remote is where you last saw it
steps.note: This rewrites remote history. --force-with-lease aborts if someone pushed since your last fetch, which plain --force does not. Never use plain --force on a shared branch. If this is a protected branch, it should be rejected by policy, not by your judgement.
steps.look: A forced update line. If it is rejected with 'stale info', someone pushed after your fetch and the lease did its job.

signals.means: The lease saved you. Someone pushed after your last fetch. Fetch again and re-examine before retrying.
Branch protection blocked it. That is working as intended; open a PR instead.

causes.cause: Other people have commits on this branch.
causes.fix: Do not force-push. Merge their work in, or coordinate a window with them first.

causes.cause: Someone pushed between your fetch and your push.
causes.fix: Fetch, inspect what arrived, rebase onto it, then retry with --force-with-lease.
Open a pull request. If the rewrite is genuinely required, it needs a repo admin, not a workaround.

verify: No commits by other authors disappeared from the log.
CI on the branch is green after the rewrite.
escalate: git log --oneline of local and remote branch
The exact push output including any rejection reason
Whether the branch is protected and who owns it
